topic: Fear response: amygdala, adrenaline, digestion, goosebumps, time slowing
hook: What fear does to your body in seconds
caption:
Fear hits your body before you even know what scared you. Your amygdala sounds the alarm first, and adrenaline handles the rest in seconds.

One strange bonus: in a 2007 experiment, people who free-fell 31 metres into a net felt the drop lasted about a third longer than it did. Their brains weren't slowing time. They were just recording more memory.

What's a scary moment you still remember in slow motion?

1/5 Your brain reacts first
Your amygdala flags danger before the thinking part of your brain even knows what it saw.
📷 Brenda Clarke from Blaxland, Australia (CC BY 2.0) via wikimedia

2/5 Adrenaline floods in
Adrenaline makes your heart pound and your breathing speed up, sending extra oxygen to your muscles.
📷 Dguendel (CC BY 4.0) via wikimedia

3/5 Your gut shuts down
Blood is pulled away from your stomach, which is why fear feels like butterflies or nausea.
📷 ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, K. Noll, J. Kastner, M. Zamani (ESA/Webb) (CC BY 4.0) via wikimedia

4/5 Goosebumps appear
Tiny muscles raise your hairs, a leftover reflex that once made furry ancestors look bigger.
📷 Sheepwalrus (CC BY-SA 4.0) via wikimedia

5/5 Time seems to slow
Fear makes your brain store denser memories, so scary moments feel longer when you remember them.
